The Scale DyT Forgot

LayerNorm has a theorem behind it. DyT has a fitted curve. This notebook asks what that missing theorem costs when the input scale moves, and answers with a trained model you can push around. Paper: "Transformers without Normalization" (Zhu, Chen, He, Yu, Yuille, LeCun, 2025, arXiv 2503.10622) replaces every LayerNorm in a transformer with one line: ||(\mathrm{DyT}(x) = \tanh(\alpha x) \odot \gamma + \beta||), where ||(\alpha||) is a single learned number per layer. It matches or beats LayerNorm across a wide range of benchmarks, and it is simpler and faster to run. It also gives up a property LayerNorm has for free: ||(\mathrm{LN}(cx) = \mathrm{LN}(x)||) for any positive constant ||(c||), exactly, by algebra. Rescale the input to a LayerNorm and nothing downstream notices. Rescale the input to a DyT layer and ||(\alpha||), frozen the moment training ends, has no way to react. Below, we train a tiny transformer twice on the same task, once with each kind of layer, then push the input off the scale it trained on and watch what breaks, and what doesn't. Why it matters: activation scale is exactly the thing that moves in deployment, through quantization, precision changes, domain shift, and long-context drift. A normalization layer that is only calibrated to one scale is a bet that none of those happen. This notebook measures the bet. (The paper's page on alphaXiv also has an AI summary and a discussion tab if you want the fast overview before the deep dive.)

The task, and the theorem

We train on the induction/copy task (Olsson et al., 2022, "In-context Learning and Induction Heads"): a random sequence of distinct tokens, then the same sequence again. To predict the next token anywhere in the second half, the model has to notice "I have seen this token before, what came right after it" and copy the answer. No download, no labeled corpus, nothing beyond a random-number generator -- and even a two-layer attention model learns it reliably. The theorem doing the work in this notebook is one line of algebra. For any input ||(x||) and scalar ||(c \neq 0||): ||[ \mathrm{LN}(cx) = \frac{cx - \mathrm{mean}(cx)}{\mathrm{std}(cx)} = \frac{c\,(x - \mathrm{mean}(x))}{|c|\cdot \mathrm{std}(x)} = \mathrm{sign}(c) \cdot \mathrm{LN}(x) ||]Mean and standard deviation both scale by ||(|c|||) and cancel. LayerNorm's output does not know or care what scale its input arrived at. DyT's ||(\tanh(\alpha x)||) has no such cancellation: it is close to linear (so close to scale-sensitive) near the origin, and it saturates to ||(\pm 1||) far from it. ||(\alpha||) was fit once, at training time, to whatever scale the activations happened to have then. It is not a normalization in the algebraic sense at all -- it is a fixed nonlinearity that happened to sit in the right place for one particular input distribution. Below: a two-dimensional stress test where the control is the result itself. The pad you drag is a heatmap of DyT's measured accuracy over the whole stress grid; every pixel under the puck is a real evaluation of the trained model. Horizontal: a global scale multiplier applied to every token. Vertical: how unevenly that scale is spread across tokens in the same sequence, an outlier-token simulator. Drag the puck and watch three views of the same trained models respond together.

What to look for

The left panel is accuracy against scale, several fixed noise levels drawn as reference curves, with a marker showing exactly where the pad sits right now. LayerNorm's curve is flat: task accuracy at 8x scale is the same as at 1x, the same as at 1/8th, because ||(\mathrm{LN}||) genuinely cannot tell the difference. DyT's curve peaks near the multiplier it was trained at and falls away on both sides, not only toward saturation -- shrinking the input shrinks ||(\tanh(\alpha x)||)'s output by roughly the same factor while it is still in the near-linear region, which throws off the relative magnitude the rest of the network learned to expect from that branch, well before anything actually saturates. The middle panel is the distribution of ||(\alpha x||) for one representative norm site (the input layer), the values tanh is about to squash, with the region where ||(|\alpha x|||) is large enough that tanh has essentially clipped shaded in red. Push the multiplier up and watch the histogram slide into that band. Push it down and the histogram huddles near zero, off the training distribution in the other direction. The right panel is the theorem itself, measured directly on a fresh random tensor with no trained weights involved: the largest difference between a norm site's output at scale ||(c||) and at scale 1. It sits at zero for LayerNorm at every multiplier we test, by construction. It grows for DyT as soon as ||(\alpha x||) leaves the linear region.
depth sweep ready: 27 independent training runs, 0 diverged

Reading the depth panel

The paper's own analysis of trained ||(\alpha||) values shows that ||(\alpha||) adapts, during training, to the scale of its own layer's activations at that depth. A frozen scalar tuned precisely to sit inside tanh's linear region for one specific training-time distribution raises a question worth testing directly: does a deeper stack of such precisely-tuned, frozen scalars leave less room for error, so the same rescale stress opens a wider gap the more layers it has to propagate through? Left panel: the fragility gap (baseline accuracy minus stressed accuracy) against depth, one line per norm, shaded band showing the spread across seeds. Right panel: the two accuracies that gap is built from, separately, dashed for baseline and solid for stressed, so a shrinking gap can be told apart from "this run simply didn't finish training." We report what the multi-seed sweep actually shows rather than what the prediction says it should show; a small-scale single-seed check made while building this notebook did not find a clean monotonic trend, and that is worth taking at face value rather than explaining away.

A fix that isn't in the paper

If DyT's problem is that ||(\alpha x||) is not scale-invariant, the direct fix is to make it scale-invariant the same way LayerNorm's argument is: divide by a per-token statistic of ||(x||) before applying ||(\alpha||). Here we divide by the per-token root-mean-square: ||(\mathrm{RMS\text{-}DyT}(x) = \tanh(\alpha \cdot x / \mathrm{rms}(x)) \cdot \gamma + \beta||). Algebraically, ||(\mathrm{rms}(cx) = |c| \cdot \mathrm{rms}(x)||) for any scalar ||(c||), global or per-token, so the multiplier cancels out of the tanh argument the same way it cancels out of LayerNorm's mean and standard deviation. The measured curve above backs this up: RMS-DyT tracks LayerNorm's flat line rather than DyT's collapsing one. That is not a free lunch. Computing a per-token RMS is a reduction over the feature dimension -- the exact operation DyT's efficiency pitch is built around removing. This candidate restores scale-invariance by re-adding the cost the paper spent its argument eliminating. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on whether the deployment setting has activation-scale drift to begin with, and the paper's own results suggest that for a great many settings, it does not.

What this does and does not show

  • The induction task, the tiny transformer, and the training loop are all synthetic and built for this notebook; nothing here downloads a checkpoint or a dataset. That buys speed and reproducibility, not a claim that these exact numbers transfer to a billion-parameter language model. The paper's own experiments, at real scale, are the place to look for that.
  • Every DyT ||(\alpha||) value in this notebook is learned by gradient descent on the unstressed task, exactly as the paper trains it, never hand-set to make a point. The fragility shown here is what training actually produces, not a worst-case ||(\alpha||) chosen to fail.
  • "Exact" invariance for LayerNorm means exact up to the ||(\epsilon = 10^{-5}||) in its denominator: the measured LayerNorm gaps in panel C sit at floating-point scale, not literally zero.
  • The rescale stress (a global multiplier times an independent per-token lognormal factor) is one specific, simple model of activation-scale drift. Real deployment-time distribution shift can look different: precision changes, sequence-length effects, domain shift, adversarial inputs. The mechanism this notebook demonstrates, a frozen scalar with no way to react to a shifted input scale, is general; the exact numbers are not a benchmark.
  • The depth sweep uses a handful of seeds per configuration, enough to see whether a trend is there, not enough to report a tight confidence interval on it.

Reproduction check

claim source measured here
✅ alpha learned by gradient descent, never hand-set paper's training recipe same (see engine)
✅ LayerNorm scale invariance LN(cx) = LN(x) exact by algebra accuracy 1.000 at 8x scale
✅ DyT matches LayerNorm on-distribution paper's benchmark claim accuracy 1.000 at training scale
⚠️ DyT under input rescale (NOT tested in the paper) no claim made accuracy falls to 0.144 at 8x: this notebook's finding
✅ RMS-DyT restores invariance predicted by the same algebra accuracy 1.000 at 8x
⚠️ fragility gap vs depth plausible hypothesis no clean monotonic trend across seeds; reported as measured
Check marks are reproductions of the paper or of the underlying algebra; warning rows are this notebook's own measurements beyond the paper's scope.

Every number above came out of this kernel. The fastest way to feel the result is to break it yourself: drag the puck to the far right of the map and watch the histogram slide into the saturation zone. Go do that.

References

  2. Olsson et al. In-context Learning and Induction Heads. 2022. arXiv 2209.11895
